chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
title: Duke tearing apart arrangements for continuity
summary: Henderson wrote commercially despite playing bebop, and Duke reworked any arrangement, jumping between letters; he told Jackson he didn't like the continuity.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Rick made a couple of good arrangements, and it was a funny thing, you know. Rick Henderson played one way but he wrote another. Now, he played be-bop saxophone to me but his writing was rather on the commercial side, you know, and to me it was an oddity. But he made good arrangements, but I don't care who would make arrangements in that band, Duke would take it and tear it apart, you know, --

-- which he would like to -- which he did, rather -- not like to, he did with his own arrangements a lot of times. You would start out with letter A and you're liable to jump over to D, maybe to F and then back to B and down here to G and back up to A, you know, and finish you out like that.

So I asked him one day, I said, "Gee whiz, Edward," I said, "why do you want to cut up an arrangement like that? It sound good the way we played it the first time down?" He said, "Well, I didn't like the continuity."
So that's the reason he would change it, you know, because I would ask. If I wanted to know, you know, I'm very inquisitive, I'll ask, you know.
That's the reason you had such advancement.
